title: Green Fenton-like Synthesis of Anion-Tunable PEDOT Conductive Powders for Flexible Bioelectronics
authors: Ziwei Jiang; Gen Wang; Xiyuan Duan; Huiyang Zhang; Ranxing Deng; Xuan-Feng Jiang; Daheng Wang; Shimin Wang
matched_keywords: bioelectronics; bioelectronic; wearable bioelectronics; conductive polymer
abstract: Abstract Conventional chemical oxidative polymerization of EDOT to produce pristine PEDOT conductive polymers has several critical drawbacks, including long reaction times, high oxidant consumption, low product purity, severe environmental pollution, and low conductivity (<1 S/cm). These limitations hinder the use of pristine PEDOT in high-performance flexible bioelectronics. In this work, we address these challenges by developing a green and efficient Fenton-like oxidative polymerization strategy using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant and a trace amount of iron salt as the catalyst. This radical-mediated process generates no harmful byproducts. The conductivity and yield of the resulting PEDOT powders are influenced by the acid dosage, reaction time, iron concentration, and oxidant amount. The resulting neutral PEDOT powders exhibit high purity, uniform particle size, good aqueous dispersibility, low residual iron content, and a moderate conductivity of 6.5 S/cm. Based on these properties, we fabricate a physically cross-linked biohydrogel through a freeze–thaw process using PEDOT powder, poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), and a small amount of tannic acid (TA). The resulting PVA/PEDOT/TA/Fe3+ hydrogel exhibits excellent stretchability, adhesion, electrical stability, and biocompatibility. Overall, this work provides a green and versatile platform for developing high-performance PEDOT-based hydrogels, with potential applications in wearable bioelectronics, including skin-mounted sensors, medical patches, and neuromuscular stimulators.

title: Biodegradable Conductors for Implantable and Wearable Transient Bioelectronics
authors: Yicheng Zhu; Yijun Liu; Naoji Matsuhisa
abstract: ABSTRACT Transient bioelectronics, as an emerging class of electronic systems, can degrade at controlled rates or within predefined time frames, thereby avoiding the risks associated with secondary surgical removal while reducing electronic waste. In biomedical applications, these systems offer new opportunities for short‐term monitoring, diagnosis, and therapy in both implantable and wearable formats. Within these systems, biodegradable conductors serve as core functional materials that enable sensing, electrical stimulation, and transmission of signals and energy, thereby determining overall device performance. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in biodegradable conductors, focusing on their degradation mechanisms and the key performance requirements for integration into transient bioelectronics. The characteristics of different classes of biodegradable conductors, including metals, conducting polymers, ionic conductors, and conductive composites, are discussed. Strategies for evaluating and regulating their functional lifetimes, as well as suitable fabrication approaches, are presented. Finally, representative biomedical applications in sensing, stimulation, energy devices, and drug delivery systems are summarized, and future perspectives for the development of transient bioelectronics are outlined.

title: Tunable Fluorescence of Graphdiyne Quantum Dots by Enlarging π System and Altering Electronic Structure
authors: Ling Qiao; Wenchao Lang; Jia Luo; Xiaoqing Xu
abstract: Extending the fluorescence of graphdiyne quantum-dot-derived materials beyond the predominantly reported blue-to-green region may broaden their use in fluorescence imaging and sensing. To address this issue, modified graphdiyne quantum dots (M-GDQDs) with green, yellow, and red fluorescence were first obtained by classical hydrothermal and solvothermal methods. Experimental and theoretical studies have shown that the enlargement of the π system and the changes in electronic structures contributed to the red shift in the fluorescence emission wavelength, although the individual contributions of conjugation and surface chemistry could not be quantitatively separated. The prepared M-GDQDs exhibit wonderful optical properties, good water solubility and excellent biocompatibility, which are beneficial for bioimaging. This study not only enriches the types of graphdiyne quantum dots, but it can also be used for the construction of multichannel fluorescent biosensing platforms. We believe that the emergence of M-GDQDs offers promising application prospects in the fields of nanomedicine and disease-related biomarker analysis.

title: Carbon Quantum Dots for Bioimaging: Advancements and Applications
abstract: Carbon quantum dots (CQDs) have emerged as versatile fluorescent nanomaterials (NMs), offering remarkable potential for high-resolution and targeted bioimaging applications due to their exceptional photostability, reduced photobleaching, facile surface functionalization, biocompatibility, and tunable optical properties. This chapter unveils the synthesis methods, structural and optical properties, fluorescence-based imaging mechanisms, and techniques for functionalizing the surface of these materials to enhance their biomedical performance. The chapter further explores various applications, including cellular imaging, fluorescence-guided surgery, and multimodal diagnostics, followed by comparing CQDs with different NMs. Lastly, clinical translational issues and the future trend of CQD-based bioimaging are discussed.

title: End-to-end deep learning for identifying Alzheimer’s disease signatures in spectral fluorescence imaging of normal-appearing brain regions in 5xFAD mice
authors: Raissa Souza; Paula J. Brandt; Anthony J. Winder; Mohammad Khazaei; Peter K. Stys; Nils D. Forkert
abstract: PurposeAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia, characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau aggregates in the brain. Current diagnostic approaches primarily detect mature plaques, but growing evidence suggests that pre-fibrillar aggregates are present earlier in normal-appearing tissue and may provide a valuable window for intervention. We propose the first proof-of-concept end-to-end deep learning (DL) model to identify AD signatures directly from normal-appearing tissue (i.e., background parenchyma) of raw spectral fluorescence data.ApproachTo develop and evaluate our DL model, we used one million signals extracted from spectral fluorescence images of brain cortex sections collected from wild-type and 5xFAD mice (a transgenic strain carrying five familial human AD mutations).ResultsOur results demonstrate that AD-related signatures can indeed be detected in normal-appearing brain cortex regions. Experiments revealed that model performance depends on input dimensions, training set size, and the preprocessing kernel size. The optimal configuration used 1000×32 input, 9000 training samples, and a 3×3 kernel, achieving ≥95% accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Importantly, no mice were misclassified, and saliency analysis indicated that a broad range of spectral fluorescence wavelengths contributed to the model’s decisions.ConclusionsThese findings highlight the potential of DL-based analysis of spectral fluorescence data to enable earlier detection of AD-related changes, supporting a shift toward a more proactive strategy for biomarker discovery.

title: Development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy using heralded emission spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials
authors: Nicola J. Fairbairn; Koya Onoda; Ozora Iso; Masahiro Yabuno; Hirotaka Terai; Shigehito Miki; Yuji Kagotani; Motoyasu Adachi; Gordon J. Hedley; Ryosuke Shimizu
abstract: Organic light-emitting materials are widely used in optoelectronics and bioimaging, but sometimes conventional fluorescence spectroscopy techniques can be limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up and photobleaching. We report a quantum-spectroscopic approach using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection, to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities. We demonstrate this approach across three organic light-emitting material classes: the fluorescent dye Rhodamine 6G, an organic semiconducting conjugated polymer poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), and a fluorescent protein mOrange. The intrinsic timing correlation between signal and idler photons enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Across all materials and integration times of 500, 1000 and 3600 seconds, heralded detection yields signal-to-noise ratios 1.6-3.0 times higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range. For MEH-PPV, this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Our measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical pulsed-laser reference values.
